how_it_wins:
Start with the number that defines this deck: zero. That is what the engine costs. Edgar Markov's eminence triggers from the command zone — every other Vampire spell you cast makes a 1/1 black Vampire token while he sits at home, untaxed and untouchable. The goldfish run (seed 42, 10,000 iterations, conservative — no interaction modeled) shows what that buys: a mean of 1.766 bodies by turn 3 and 4.111 by turn 6, on a curve that stacks 8 one-drops and 18 each at two and three. And in v2 the bodies themselves became ammunition twice over: Purphoros, God of the Forge turns every entry into 2 damage to each opponent — stack 008 verified that one two-mana Vampire cast through both doublers is five entry triggers, 10 damage to every opponent — and the aristocrats layer (Viscera Seer, Cruel Celebrant, Grave Pact) converts each spare token into a scry, a table-wide drain, and an edict on its way out. You are the beatdown by default, and a sweeper now costs the table almost as much as it costs you.

Combat reach is the each-opponent drain, verified at both ends of the turn. Stack 003: seven attacking Vampires under Sanctum Seeker and Bloodletter of Aclazotz drain each opponent 14 at declare-attackers, before blockers exist. Stack 007: the same seven tapped bodies drain each opponent another 14 at your end step through Throne of the God-Pharaoh — with the honest bound its own artifact insists on: that end-step trigger is not a table-kill (a 15-life opponent survives it at exactly 1), and the 28-per-opponent full-turn figure is arithmetic composition of two separately verified artifacts, not one verified line. A drain engine is drawn by turn 6 in 62.7% of games; a lord or Vampire payoff in 66.3%; a token amplifier in 42.2%, and stack 002's math still governs the doubler turns: one two-mana Vampire cast becomes five bodies through Anointed Procession and Mondrak.

The headline change of v2: the infinite graduated from insurance to co-equal plan. The deck now holds a 2x2 kill-web — two lose-halves (Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose; Sanguine Bond) times two gain-halves (Exquisite Blood; Bloodthirsty Conqueror) — and all four pairings are checker-verified deterministic table-kills (stacks 001, 004, 005, 006), each a zero-mana loop once both pieces are down. Natural assembly of any pair is 5.4% by turn 6 and 9.4% by turn 10 with tutors unmodeled, and Demonic Tutor, Vampiric Tutor, and Diabolic Intent each count as a copy of whichever half you're missing. Sequencing is now a skill of its own: stack 005's pairing — Sanguine Bond plus Exquisite Blood, both enchantments — is the one instant-speed creature removal cannot break, so when the table holds up mana, tutor toward that pairing first. Redundancy, not any single combo, is what the seven swaps bought: for the first time the game that goes long is often your game.

Edgar himself is still the pivot, not the opener. His goldfish median cast is turn 6 (mean 6.628, 51.2% by turn 6), and the correct pivot is casting him the turn you alpha-strike: his attack trigger puts a +1/+1 counter on every Vampire you control, converting an accumulated token board into lethal width. Hold protection for exactly that turn — Akroma's Will, Boros Charm, Flawless Maneuver; a protection piece is held by turn 6 in 57.5% of games — and remember the tension the strategic frame names: Deflecting Swat and Flawless Maneuver are free only while you control a commander, which is precisely what the eminence plan delays. Beat down, drain wide, burn every cast through Purphoros, and finish with whichever half of the web the table failed to answer.

combo_lines.001: The deck's bracket-4 backbone, verified end to end against the June 19, 2026 comprehensive rules over a 10-step resolution. The scene: Exquisite Blood and Vito on your battlefield, and Vampire Nighthawk's lifelink has just gained you 2 off combat damage. That 2-life seed is all the loop needs. Vito's trigger drains a target opponent, Exquisite Blood gains it back, Vito triggers again — and because each Vito trigger is a new object whose target you choose fresh as it goes on the stack, you walk the drain across the table in any order. The checker confirmed the parts people argue about: the loop is shortcut-legal, a targeted opponent dying mid-loop does not break the chain (their killing life loss still triggers your enchantment, which targets nothing), and from this board it takes exactly 38 Vito resolutions — 6, 13, and 19 — to clear opponents at 12, 25, and 38 life. You end at 105 life, having spent no mana and no cards, and win by rule 104.2a the moment the last opponent leaves.
combo_lines.002: The token-math stack, and the one to internalize because it runs every turn, not just combo turns. You cast Gifted Aetherborn for {B}{B} with Edgar still in the command zone and both doublers out. Eminence triggers once — one token event — and Anointed Procession and Mondrak each double it in whichever order you like (the checker confirmed the result is identical: 1 becomes 2 becomes 4). Those four 1/1s each enter carrying a Vampire Socialite counter because an opponent lost life this turn, and the Aetherborn itself arrives as a 3/4. Net: five new Vampire bodies off one two-mana spell. Just as important is what does not happen: eminence does not re-trigger on the tokens (they are created, not cast), and Cordial Vampire stays silent because nothing died. This is the multiplication table behind the goldfish's body counts — know it cold before you commit to a doubler turn.
combo_lines.003: The drain math that makes go-wide combat real against three opponents, verified at the moment of declare-attackers. Seven Vampires attack — Bloodletter, Sanctum Seeker, four eminence tokens, and a hasty Edgar — and Sanctum Seeker triggers once per attacking Vampire: seven triggers. It is your turn, so Bloodletter's replacement doubles each opponent's loss per trigger event: every opponent loses 2, seven times, for 14 total. Your gain is not doubled — Bloodletter reads opponents' life loss only — so you gain 7. The checker confirmed the brutal part: the opponent at 14 hits exactly 0 on the seventh trigger and is eliminated by state-based actions before blockers are ever declared, and because you control the remaining triggers, an opponent's death never strands them. Edgar's own attack trigger has already put a counter on all seven bodies. This is 14 damage per opponent for the cost of turning creatures sideways.
combo_lines.004: The second corner of what is now a 2x2 kill-web, verified on its own terms rather than by analogy — the strategic frame insisted, and it was right to. Bloodthirsty Conqueror's trigger matches Exquisite Blood's word for word, and the checker confirmed its '(Damage causes loss of life.)' parenthetical is reminder text, not a damage requirement: Vito's direct life loss triggers it just fine. From a 3-life seed the loop runs exactly as stack 001 did — deterministic, shortcut-legal, retargetable each iteration, unbroken by a mid-loop death — and kills a 9-life and a 30-life opponent in 13 Vito resolutions with zero overkill, leaving you at 60. The honest cost is the difference: Conqueror is a 5/5 creature, and every iteration's priority window admits instant-speed creature removal as a loop-breaker, making this pairing strictly more fragile than the all-enchantment lines. Its flying and deathtouch contribute nothing to the loop — they are for the fair game this card also happens to dominate.
combo_lines.005: The pairing the seven swaps were built around, and the most resilient corner of the web: Sanguine Bond plus Exquisite Blood, both enchantments. Bond's trigger is word-for-word Vito's first ability — 'Whenever you gain life, target opponent loses that much life' — and this stack verified the swap before it was applied: from a 2-life lifelink seed, 26 Bond resolutions (9 for the opponent at 17, then 17 for the opponent at 34) clear the table, retargeting each fresh trigger as it goes on the stack. The chain crosses deaths — the first opponent's killing loss still triggers Exquisite Blood — and you win via rule 104.2a at 79 life, the final Exquisite Blood trigger mooted by the win itself. What makes this the pairing to tutor toward when the table holds up mana: there is no creature in the loop, so the per-iteration instant-speed removal window that stacks 004 and 006 must confess to simply does not exist here. Swords, Deluge, and every edict in the room read this loop and find nothing to touch.
combo_lines.006: The pairing that closes the 2x2: Sanguine Bond plus Bloodthirsty Conqueror, verified in 9 steps on the same terms as its three siblings. From a 3-life seed, 13 Bond resolutions kill the table — 4 for the opponent at 11, then 9 for the opponent at 26, each overkilling by exactly 1 because 3 divides neither total (unlike stack 004's clean zeros). The dying opponent's killing loss still triggers Conqueror, so the chain crosses their death, and the 13th Conqueror trigger is mooted by your immediate 104.2a win; you end at 58 life with the loop having consumed no cards, mana, or creatures. The removal-window profile sits between its siblings: exactly one creature half, so every iteration offers instant-speed creature removal one target — but only one, where stack 004's pairing offers two. Know this line so that whichever half the tutor finds first, you already know what completes it.
combo_lines.007: The honest one — read this intro as a warning label, because this stack is a verified 14-per-opponent drain and a partially refuted table-kill, and its own artifact says so. The scene is the turn stack 003 built: seven attackers now tapped after combat, Throne of the God-Pharaoh out, Bloodletter untapped because it stayed home. At your end step Throne triggers — each opponent loses life equal to your tapped creatures — and the checker confirmed both halves of the math: the untapped Bloodletter does not count itself toward the seven, but the end step is still your turn, so its replacement doubles each opponent's loss independently. Each opponent loses 14, not 7. That killed the 9-life opponent (to -5, gone via state-based actions) — and the 15-life opponent survived at exactly 1, the game continuing in your own end step. Never present this as lethal-by-default: it is a second 14-per-opponent installment on the attack turn's arithmetic, and the 28-per-opponent full-turn figure is a composition of two separately verified artifacts, not itself a checker-passed line.
combo_lines.008: The reason Purphoros made the 99, resolved trigger by trigger. You cast a two-mana Vampire with Edgar in the command zone and Anointed Procession, Mondrak, and Purphoros on the battlefield. The eminence event doubles twice — stack 002's verified 1-2-4 — and the checker confirmed the part that decides the damage: four tokens entering simultaneously is one event with four occurrences, which means four separate Purphoros triggers, plus a fifth when the spell's own body resolves and enters. Five triggers, 2 damage each, to every opponent: 10 per head per two-mana cast. Purphoros's devotion clause is irrelevant to its own trigger (and note your lifelink creatures gain you nothing here — Purphoros dealt the damage, not they). In the verified line the opponent at 10 hits exactly 0 on the fifth trigger's resolution and loses to the state-based check; had they died earlier, the remaining triggers would still have resolved against the survivor. This is the card that turns the goldfish's body counts into a clock that ignores blockers entirely.

card_roles.Edgar Markov: The engine that never needs to be cast: eminence makes a 1/1 Vampire per other Vampire spell from the command zone, all game, for free. When he does arrive (goldfish median turn 6), cast him as the alpha-strike pivot — his attack trigger puts a +1/+1 counter on every Vampire you control, and first strike plus haste means he leads the charge the turn he lands.
card_roles.Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose: One of the kill-web's two lose-halves: every life gain becomes targeted life loss, and stacks 001 and 004 verified his loops with each gain-half. He dies on sight at bracket 4, which is exactly why Sanguine Bond exists as his redundant twin. Even bare, he converts each lifelink hit and Sanctum Seeker gain into damage, and his activated ability grants the whole team lifelink for one drain-everything combat.
card_roles.Sanguine Bond: The second lose-half, word-for-word Vito's first ability on an enchantment — and the piece that turns the combo from a two-pairing into a 2x2 web. Stacks 005 and 006 verified its loops with both gain-halves, and the 005 pairing with Exquisite Blood is the deck's most resilient kill: two enchantments, no creature for instant-speed removal to touch mid-loop.
card_roles.Exquisite Blood: Gain-half number one, and the more resilient of the two — no creature removal touches it. It closes verified loops with both lose-halves (stack 001 with Vito, stack 005 with Sanguine Bond), and the Bond pairing is the all-enchantment line to tutor toward when the table holds up mana. Fair-game mode: every point of drain your engines inflict comes back as life.
card_roles.Bloodthirsty Conqueror: Gain-half number two, verified with both lose-halves (stack 004 with Vito, stack 006 with Bond) — same loops, but exposed to creature removal every iteration. As a fair card it is a 5/5 flying deathtouch body that turns every opponent life loss into gain; the frame's advice stands: do not trade a loop half in combat.
card_roles.Sanctum Seeker: The go-wide payoff stack 003 verified: each attacking Vampire drains every opponent for 1 and gains you 1. Seven attackers under Bloodletter is 14 from each opponent before blocks — this is the card that makes token combat scale against three life totals.
card_roles.Bloodletter of Aclazotz: Doubles every opponent's life loss on your turn — drains, combat damage, edict aftermath, all of it. Stack 003 shows the effect at declare-attackers (seven Sanctum Seeker triggers become 14 per opponent), and stack 007 shows it again at your end step, doubling Throne's trigger to another 14 — remembering that an untapped Bloodletter does not count itself among the tapped.
card_roles.Throne of the God-Pharaoh: Two mana that makes every attack echo: at your end step, each opponent loses life equal to your tapped creatures, and Bloodletter doubles it (stack 007: seven tapped attackers, 14 per opponent). Carry the artifact's own caveat — it is verified reach, not a table-kill; a 15-life opponent survives the trigger at exactly 1. It also pays off boards that attacked into blockers or got wrathed after combat: tapped is tapped.
card_roles.Purphoros, God of the Forge: The token engine's damage converter, verified in stack 008: one two-mana Vampire cast through both doublers is five entry triggers — 10 damage to each opponent. Indestructible, and usually a noncreature at this deck's red devotion, so it shrugs off creature wraths while triggering fully. The named cost: he is not a Vampire, so his own cast banks no eminence token and no lord buffs him.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: The deck's one true sac outlet, and the aristocrats layer's ignition switch: sacrifice any creature at instant speed to scry 1. Each free eminence token becomes an on-demand death — a Grave Pact edict, a Cruel Celebrant drain, a Cordial Vampire counter — with card selection stapled on, and it makes Voldaren Pariah's three-creature flip castable on your terms. All on a one-mana Vampire that banks its own eminence token on the way in.
card_roles.Cruel Celebrant: The aristocrats payoff: every creature or planeswalker of yours that dies costs each opponent 1 life and gains you 1. With Seer providing the deaths, spare tokens become table-wide drains — and that gain-1 is a live seed for any assembled loop pairing (stacks 005 and 006 both ignite from exactly such a gain), which means a full pair on the battlefield turns even a wrath into the kill.
card_roles.Kalitas, Traitor of Ghet: The defensive anchor the swaps bought back: a lifelink four-drop whose replacement effect exiles opponents' dying nontoken creatures — no death triggers, no reanimation — and mints you a 2/2 Zombie each time, which is itself Seer fodder or food for Kalitas's own counter-stacking sac ability. In a deck forcing edicts with Grave Pact, his text is live in every game.
card_roles.Twilight Prophet: With the city's blessing (trivial here), every upkeep reveals the top card, drains each opponent for its mana value, and puts it in your hand — card advantage and reach in one body, and every gain is a lose-half trigger.
card_roles.Bontu's Monument: Cost reducer for the deck's two dozen black creature spells that also drains each opponent for 1 (and gains you 1 — a lose-half trigger) on every creature cast. On an 18-and-18 two/three-drop curve, the discount is real velocity.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: The velocity engine: Vampire spells cost {1} less — a rebate on nearly every cast in a 29-body list — and each upkeep peeks the top card, pocketing it if it's a Vampire. It is why the ramp-or-fixing goldfish target sits at 50.2% by turn 6 in v2, and the frame calls it the best turn-3 noncreature play: every discounted cast is still an eminence token.
card_roles.Legion Lieutenant: The cleanest lord: other Vampires get +1/+1, turning eminence 1/1s into 2/2s for two mana.
card_roles.Stromkirk Captain: Lord plus first strike for the whole tribe — the card that lets 2/2 tokens trade up and lets your swarm play defense against faster aggro seats.
card_roles.Captivating Vampire: A lord with a lategame mode: tap five Vampires (tokens gladly) to steal the table's best creature permanently — and it becomes a Vampire under your lords.
card_roles.Bloodline Keeper // Lord of Lineage: A token per turn from the tap ability, and at five Vampires — easy with eminence — it transforms into a 5/5 flying +2/+2 lord that keeps making 2/2 fliers.
card_roles.Drana, Liberator of Malakir: First strike means her combat damage lands early, putting a +1/+1 counter on every attacking creature before regular damage is even dealt — a mid-combat anthem on a 2/3 flying body.
card_roles.Vampire Socialite: In this deck an opponent has nearly always lost life, so every later Vampire enters with an extra counter — stack 002's four tokens arrived as 2/2s because of her. Menace makes her a fine early attacker to switch the ability on.
card_roles.Cordial Vampire: Every creature death — yours, theirs, anyone's — puts a counter on each Vampire you control. Alongside Grave Pact, Viscera Seer, and your own edict effects, board wipes aimed at you leave the survivors bigger.
card_roles.Shared Animosity: Every attacker shares a type with every other attacker here, so each one gets +1/+0 per fellow attacker — width converted directly into power. Seven attackers is +6 apiece.
card_roles.Vanquisher's Banner: Name Vampire: an anthem plus a card for every Vampire spell you cast — with the curve's cheap casts, it refills as fast as you deploy.
card_roles.Cover of Darkness: Choose Vampire and the swarm gains fear — blockable only by artifact and/or black creatures. The card that turns a stalled board into lethal width.
card_roles.Akroma's Will: The premier swing-turn spell: with Edgar on the battlefield (command zone does not count) you take both modes — flying, vigilance, double strike AND lifelink, indestructible, protection from each colour. Every lifelink point is a lose-half trigger.
card_roles.Anointed Procession: Token doubler number one, verified in stack 002: with Mondrak also out, each eminence trigger makes four tokens instead of one — and stack 008 prices what that means under Purphoros. It doubles Black Market Connections' Treasures and Strefan's Blood too.
card_roles.Mondrak, Glory Dominus: Token doubler number two from stack 002, on a 4/4 body that can buy itself an indestructible counter by sacrificing two spare tokens — a doubler that survives the sweeper it invites.
card_roles.Mavren Fein, Dusk Apostle: A free lifelink token every combat your nontoken Vampires attack — steady width, and the lifelink token's gains feed the lose-halves and Ocelot Pride.
card_roles.Ocelot Pride: You gain life constantly here, so this makes a Cat every end step — and with the city's blessing it then copies every token that entered this turn. After an eminence-heavy turn, that clause is a second token doubler.
card_roles.Strefan, Maurer Progenitor: Your drains make every player lose life, so Strefan banks multiple Blood tokens per turn cycle — then his attack cashes two of them to put a Vampire from hand onto the battlefield tapped, attacking, and indestructible. Bloodletter and Conqueror love arriving free.
card_roles.Preacher of the Schism: Attacks into the life leader for a lifelink token, or — once your drains put you on top — draws a card per attack instead. A deathtouch 2/4 that opponents hate blocking either way.
card_roles.Welcoming Vampire: A card per turn whenever another power-2-or-less creature enters — every eminence token switches it on. One of the deck's steadiest draw engines (a draw engine is held by turn 6 in 50.6% of goldfish runs).
card_roles.Black Market Connections: The premium life-priced engine: Treasure, cards, or a 3/2 changeling — which is a Vampire, so it counts for lords and Sanctum Seeker. Life is cheap early currency in a deck that gains it back by the dozen.
card_roles.Bloodghast: Sweeper insurance and edict fodder that returns on every landfall — including fetch activations. It can't block, so spend it freely on Viscera Seer, Diabolic Intent, and Grave Pact math.
card_roles.Knight of the Ebon Legion: The best one-drop in the tribe: a pump activation to trade up, and a free +1/+1 counter every end step someone lost 4 or more life — a bar this deck's drains clear constantly.
card_roles.Vampire of the Dire Moon: One mana, deathtouch, lifelink: an early attacker deterrent whose every connected point is a lose-half trigger — and, after the swaps, the deck's only remaining one-drop deathtouch defender, so value its body accordingly.
card_roles.Nighthawk Scavenger: A 1+X flier with deathtouch and lifelink, where X is the card types in opponents' graveyards — usually a 4-6 power evasive lifelinker by the mid-game, and the deck's main deathtouch blocker now that the cheap ones sit on the bench.
card_roles.Henrika Domnathi // Henrika, Infernal Se: A modal engine: each-player edict, draw, or transform into a 3/4 flying deathtouch lifelink body that pumps your evasive attackers. Take the sacrifice mode while your board is tokens and theirs is one big threat.
card_roles.Voldaren Pariah // Abolisher of Bloodlin: Three spare tokens flip her into a 6/5 flier that forces a target opponent to sacrifice three creatures of their choice — a one-sided board attack madness can cast at a discount, and Viscera Seer makes the flip cost instant-speed easy.
card_roles.Sorin, Imperious Bloodlord: The -3 cheats Bloodletter or Bloodthirsty Conqueror onto the battlefield on turn three; until then, +1 hands a Vampire deathtouch, lifelink, and a counter, or sacrifices a token for 3 damage and 3 life — which is also a lose-half trigger.
card_roles.Grave Pact: Every token death forces each opponent to sacrifice a creature — and Viscera Seer now supplies those deaths on demand at instant speed, making this a repeatable table-wide edict engine while Cordial Vampire and Cruel Celebrant profit off the same deaths.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: Premium one-mana exile; the life their creature's controller gains is a fair price for answering the table's best threat.
card_roles.Path to Exile: The second one-mana exile; the basic land it hands over matters less than the threat it removes.
card_roles.Despark: Two mana to exile any permanent at mana value four or more — the answer to the doublers, wraths-on-a-stick, and commanders the deck otherwise can't touch.
card_roles.Fracture: Two mana, instant speed, kills an artifact, enchantment, or planeswalker — the flexible answer slot for stax pieces and problem enchantments.
card_roles.Rite of Oblivion: Sacrifice a spare token to exile any nonland permanent — twice, with flashback. Eminence makes the additional cost nearly free.
card_roles.Winds of Abandon: Spot exile early, one-sided board wipe on overload late — the deck's clean answer to opposing swarms that leaves your own board untouched.
card_roles.Olivia's Wrath: The asymmetric sweeper: every non-Vampire gets -X/-X where X is your Vampire count. With a wide board it wipes the table and misses your entire army.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: The scalable sweeper: pay life to set X. It hits your own team too, so size it to kill their board while your lords keep the counters-and-anthems survivors alive — or just reset a board you can rebuild faster than anyone.
card_roles.Boros Charm: Three modes, one you'll cast most: permanents you control gain indestructible — the two-mana answer to the sweeper your token board invites. Four to the face closes games the drains started.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free indestructible — but only while you control a commander, which means it costs a real {2}{W} for every turn Edgar stays home. Budget for that tension; it's the deck's central protection trade-off.
card_roles.Deflecting Swat: Free redirection under the same commander condition as Flawless Maneuver: once Edgar is out, it bounces removal off your combo pieces or steals a tutor. Before then, it's a three-mana trick.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The total out: life locked, protection from everything, board phased out. It beats any wrath, any combo turn pointed at you, and any lethal swing — hold it for the disaster, not the inconvenience.
card_roles.Swiftfoot Boots: Hexproof and haste for one to equip — Edgar swings the turn he lands, protected, which is exactly the pivot the strategic frame says to build.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: The best tutor ever printed, and the card that turns a 9.4%-by-turn-10 natural pairing into a line you choose. With four loop halves in the 99, it is effectively a copy of whichever half — or answer — the game demands.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Top-of-library tutoring at instant speed for one mana and 2 life — set up the missing loop half or the sweeper the turn before you need it.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: Demonic Tutor priced at one creature — and eminence prints the currency. Sacrificing a token to find a loop half is this deck's cleanest exchange rate.
card_roles.Night's Whisper: Two cards for two mana and 2 life — efficient fuel, with the life loss trivially recouped by the drain suite.
card_roles.Sol Ring: The format's fastest start; a turn-one Ring is two extra mana toward double-spelling Vampires every turn after.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any Mardu colour, no drawback — the premium rock in a three-colour, colour-hungry deck.
card_roles.Talisman of Indulgence: Black or red on demand at a point of pain, colourless for free — a rock that prioritizes the deck's heaviest pip colours.
card_roles.Nomad Outpost: All three colours, enters tapped — the ingestion fix recorded in HISTORY.md: it replaced Crosis's Catacombs, whose blue identity was illegal under Edgar.
card_roles.Savai Triome: The other tapped tri-land, with a late-game upgrade: cycle it for a card when the mana is settled.
card_roles.Luxury Suite: Untapped black-red with two or more opponents — a free dual in every Commander game.
card_roles.Spectator Seating: Untapped red-white in multiplayer — same deal as Luxury Suite, no cost in practice.
card_roles.Vault of Champions: Untapped white-black in multiplayer — the third bond land, covering the deck's heaviest colour pair.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Shock land: pay 2 life for untapped black-red the turn it matters. This deck buys life back with interest.
card_roles.Godless Shrine: Shock land for the deck's core white-black pair — pay the 2 when the curve demands it.
card_roles.Sacred Foundry: The red-white shock — least-taxed of the three, since red is only 8 pips deep here.
card_roles.Arid Mesa: Fetches Mountain or Plains duals — and every fetch activation is a landfall trigger for Bloodghast.
card_roles.Bloodstained Mire: Fetches Swamp or Mountain types, including the shocks — fixing plus a free Bloodghast return.
card_roles.Marsh Flats: Fetches Plains or Swamp types — the fetch aimed at the deck's most important colour pair.
card_roles.Prismatic Vista: Fetches any basic untapped — with only five basics, crack it early while targets remain.
card_roles.Caves of Koilos: Painless colourless or white-black at 1 damage — reliable early, cheap late.
card_roles.Battlefield Forge: The red-white painland: colourless for free, coloured at a point.
card_roles.Sulfurous Springs: The black-red painland — one damage is nothing next to what the drains recoup.
card_roles.Concealed Courtyard: Untapped white-black through the first three land drops — exactly when the 8-one-drop, 18-two-drop curve needs it.
card_roles.Haunted Ridge: Black-red, untapped once you control two other lands — a mid-game dual that rarely costs tempo.
card_roles.Shattered Sanctum: White-black on the same two-other-lands condition — untapped in the turns that matter.
card_roles.Sundown Pass: Red-white with the two-other-lands clause — the least-stressed pair, so the occasional tapped turn is fine.
card_roles.Blazemire Verge: Black, or red if you control a Swamp or Mountain — in this manabase, effectively an untapped dual from turn two.
card_roles.Bleachbone Verge: Black, or white with a Plains or Swamp about — same low-cost dual design, aimed at the core pair.
card_roles.Silent Clearing: White or black at a life, and when the game floods, sacrifice it for a card — a land that never goes dead.
card_roles.Sunbaked Canyon: The red-white horizon land: pain mana early, a fresh card late.
card_roles.Mana Confluence: Any colour at 1 life per tap — the best fixing in the deck, priced in a resource the drains replenish.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: Any type your other lands could produce — with this many duals and tri-lands, it is a painless rainbow.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two colourless at 2 damage — a turn-one Tomb into a two-drop plus eminence token is one of the deck's fastest openings.
card_roles.Castle Locthwain: Black mana that becomes a life-priced draw engine when your hand empties — and this curve empties hands fast.
card_roles.Minas Tirith: White mana, usually untapped (fifteen legendary permanents here), that draws a card whenever you attacked with two or more creatures — a bar this deck clears every combat.
card_roles.Cori Mountain Monastery: Red mana with a late-game impulse draw stapled on — four mana for an extra card when the board is stable.
card_roles.Takenuma, Abandoned Mire: A Swamp that channels back a fallen creature — cheaper for each legendary you control — recovering a loop half or lord after removal without ever being a dead draw.
card_roles.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: Every land becomes a Swamp — the patch for a manabase carrying 50 black pips across 36 black cards. Your painlands and white sources all tap for black under it.
card_roles.Agadeem's Awakening // Agadeem, the Unde: A black land (pay 3 life or enter tapped) that hides a mass reanimation X-spell — the single best post-sweeper rebuild card in the deck, returning a stack of different-cost Vampires at once.
card_roles.Midgar, City of Mako // Reactor Raid: A tapped black land that can instead be cast to trade a spare token for two cards — then played as the land from exile later. Both halves fit a deck rich in expendable bodies.
card_roles.Plains: The lone white basic — the Prismatic Vista and Path to Exile target.
card_roles.Swamp: Four copies: the fetchable, Urborg-independent backbone of a 50-black-pip manabase.

mulligan:
Run the engine-hand test the strategic frame prescribes: your enablers are cheap Vampire spells and your payoffs are lords, drain pieces, and loop halves — keep enabler-heavy hands, ship payoff-heavy ones. The classic all-payoff mulligan in v2 is the seductive one: two loop halves and no cheap Vampires does nothing for four turns and telegraphs your kill to boot. Concretely, keep two to four lands (the goldfish's own mulligan rule keeps 2-5, and 81.7% of first sevens pass; kept hands cluster at 2-4 lands) plus at least two Vampires you can cast in the first three turns. Those casts are worth double — a body and an eminence token each, and with the aristocrats layer maindecked, every token is now also stored value: a future scry, edict, and drain. The payoffs find themselves: a lord or Vampire payoff is drawn by turn 6 in 66.3% of games and a drain engine in 62.7%, so you never need to mulligan toward them. One noncreature card upgrades a marginal keep: Herald's Horn — the frame's best turn-3 play — discounts every body behind it and digs a Vampire off the top each upkeep, which is why ramp-or-fixing now reaches 50.2% by turn 6.

Never keep a hand for Edgar and never mourn his absence — he lives in the command zone, and the engine runs at full power while he sits there. Ship: zero-or-one-land hands, five-plus-land hands, and any hand whose spells all cost four or more, which does nothing for three turns in a deck built to bank a token per turn from turn one or two. One nuance from deck-facts: 16 of the 34 lands can enter tapped, so a two-land keep wants at least one land that comes in untapped for the one-drop start. Protection (held by turn 6 in 57.5% of runs) and a tutor are luxuries in an opener, not requirements — the free mulligan exists, and this deck at six cards with a working curve beats seven cards of top-end every time.
upgrades:
The nine-swap analysis this section used to preview is now history — the deck you are holding is the result. The v1 bench analysis ranked nine forward-looking swaps under a recorded mandate (engine-extending picks only, verify before believing), and four of its claims were exactly the kind this manual refuses to print unverified: the two Sanguine Bond loops, the Throne-under-Bloodletter doubling, and the Purphoros per-entry count. So the verifications ran first. All four passed the checker at iteration 1 — stacks 005, 006, 007 (with its honest partially-refuted-as-a-table-kill bound), and 008 — and on 2026-07-28 the seven surviving swaps were applied: Viscera Seer, Sanguine Bond, Cruel Celebrant, Purphoros, Kalitas, Herald's Horn, and Throne of the God-Pharaoh in; Vampire Interloper, Stensia Masquerade, Gifted Aetherborn, Akroma's Memorial, Vampire Nighthawk, Ivora, and Blade of the Bloodchief to the bench. Every delta computed 4-to-4: the floor never moved, because the upgrade was never about the floor — it was redundancy on the kill (four verified pairings where v1 had two, all through-verified) and velocity to reach it, which per the bracket barometers is the real power move inside bracket 4.

What remains on the bench is now two tiers. The conditional tier is Elenda, the Dusk Rose and Indulgent Aristocrat, the two swaps from the old analysis deliberately not applied. Elenda (in for Mavren Fein) is the aristocrats package's wrath-math payoff — counters off every death anywhere, dying into a doubled army of lifelink tokens — and belongs in the list once your pods punish wide boards hard enough that threats must replace themselves. Indulgent Aristocrat (in for Vampire of the Dire Moon) is outlet redundancy once Viscera Seer proves out, at the named cost of the deck's last one-drop deathtouch defender — which is why it was the ninth swap and not the second, and why the thinned-defense tension the strategic frame flags argues for patience here. The seven fresh cuts sit beside them, and two are worth remembering at aggro-heavy tables: Gifted Aetherborn and Vampire Nighthawk are exactly the cheap deathtouch wall the swaps thinned, and re-boarding one is the natural meta call if your fair-combat seat keeps getting run over (a coaching judgment, not a computed one). Finally, four bench slots are spares, not options: a second Strefan, a second Vito, and two printings each of Vampire Nocturnus and Unholy Officiant — backup copies, sitting in the box.
threat_assessment:
You do not get a quiet game, and version 2 stopped pretending you wanted one. A bracket-4 table reads Edgar Markov from seat assignment: eminence tokens from turn 1 make 'I haven't done anything' unsellable (goldfish v2: 1.8 bodies by turn 3, 4.1 by turn 6 with zero mana spent on the commander), and the strategic frame is blunt that your deflection budget is largely pre-spent — deflection buys single turns now, not phases. But the bigger v2 change is what the table is right to fear: this deck is overtly combo-adjacent, holding a verified 2×2 kill matrix — lose-halves (Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose; Sanguine Bond) × gain-halves (Exquisite Blood; Bloodthirsty Conqueror) — all four pairings checker-passed as deterministic full-table kills: stack 001 (Exquisite+Vito, 38 iterations), 004 (Conqueror+Vito, 13), 005 (Bond+Exquisite, 26), 006 (Bond+Conqueror, 13). These are the most famous drain pairings in the format (~355k combined popularity per the frame), so the table plays against the loop from turn zero — and at this floor, sandbagging the combo reads as bad faith, not deflection. Play it honestly as a co-equal plan.

What gets answered first: every visible half, on sight. Your counter-skill is sequencing by removal-window profile, because the four pairings are not equally fragile: stack 005's Bond+Exquisite is the resilient line — both halves enchantments, no per-iteration creature-removal window — while 001, 004, and 006 each include a creature half, and 004/006's own artifacts name the per-iteration instant-speed removal window as the honest cost. So the tutors fetch toward the pairing the table's open mana cannot answer: against creature-removal-heavy seats, Sanguine Bond is the premier lose-half target and Exquisite Blood its partner; the creature halves are for tables that are tapped out or hold only enchantment-blind interaction. The tutors themselves remain your concealment — the fetched half in hand cannot be answered, and never present a pair into the open-mana window that beats it.

Second-tier answers the table will aim: the drain engines (Sanctum Seeker, Bloodletter of Aclazotz — stack 003's seven attackers is 14 per opponent at declare), Grave Pact, and now Purphoros, God of the Forge — though Purphoros is indestructible and usually not a creature, so most tables simply cannot answer him, and stack 008 verified the reach: with both doublers out, one two-mana Vampire cast is five entry triggers for 10 damage to each opponent. Throne of the God-Pharaoh adds a verified end-step echo — after a seven-attacker turn with Bloodletter out it drained 14 from each opponent (stack 007) — but it is a once-per-turn pulse, explicitly NOT a table-kill; present it as reach math, never as a loop.

Edgar himself: unchanged discipline. Keep him zoned — eminence functions from the command zone by its own terms (CR 113.6b) — and the goldfish says the honest cast is late: mean 6.628, median 6, 51.2% by turn 6 on 5.34 mean available mana. Cast him the turn he converts the board (haste plus the +1/+1-counter attack trigger), which is also the turn Flawless Maneuver and Deflecting Swat become free. Embrace archenemy on the turn it kills a player — and v2 softened the cost of wearing the label: the aristocrats layer (Viscera Seer, Cruel Celebrant, Grave Pact) monetizes the retaliatory wrath, and the enchantment halves plus Purphoros survive it outright.
matchups:
VS SWEEPER CONTROL: The wrath now costs them more than it costs you. Grave Pact and Cruel Celebrant convert the board they sweep into edicts and each-opponent drains, Viscera Seer turns dying tokens into selection, the two enchantment halves and indestructible Purphoros survive outright, and eminence rebuilds at one token per cast with no recast tax (Bloodghast returns on a land drop for free). Still commit only what wins — 'commit exactly as much as wins before it arrives, no further' (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math) — and time commitment to protection, held in 57.5% of goldfish games by turn 6. The v1 advice to fear the long game is repealed: with four verified pairings and three tutors, your inevitability is real, and against draw-go you may play the patient game they think they own. The unrebuildable loss is still Edgar — a died commander recasts at 8 (CR 903.8) — so the free Flawless Maneuver window his presence enables is for the turn you commit. Olivia's Wrath remains your own asymmetric sweeper.

VS LIFEGAIN HATE: A 'players can't gain life' effect turns off the ENTIRE 2×2 matrix — every pairing needs a gain-half to fire — and blanks the lifelink bodies. Your hate-proof plan is now three-layered and verified: Sanctum Seeker's each-opponent loss trigger doubled by Bloodletter (stack 003: seven attackers = 14 per opponent at declare, before damage), Throne of the God-Pharaoh's end-step echo (stack 007: another 14 per opponent off the same seven-attacker turn — a pulse, not a kill), and Purphoros, whose entry damage involves no lifegain at all (stack 008: 10 per opponent per two-mana Vampire through both doublers). Against a hate piece, the tutors stop fetching combo halves and start fetching the answer — or Purphoros, who ignores the hate entirely. The drain engine was drawn by turn 6 in 62.7% of goldfish runs; the fallback is the plan you usually have.

VS STAX: You are the forced beatdown, unchanged. The 18+18 two/three-drop core is exactly the many-cheap-spells profile Sphere effects halve, and the mana is already tight — 16 of 34 lands enter tapped, land-drop rate falls to 58.2% by turn 6, mean available mana 5.34 on turn 6. Race the lock's assembly and aim Despark/Fracture/Rite of Oblivion at the piece that beats YOU (usually the per-cast tax, since eminence pays per cast). Two v2 hedges: Herald's Horn rebates one generic mana on every Vampire spell — a real if narrow counter-tax — and the loops themselves are notably stax-resistant once assembled, because every pairing has mana_value_needed 0: pieces cost mana, iterations cost none. Edgar stays zoned longest here.

VS FASTER COMBO: Answer economy inverts — the last profitable moment for held interaction is now — but your counter-clock is materially faster than v1's: natural pair assembly is 5.4% by turn 6 and 9.4% by turn 10 (goldfish v2, tutors unmodeled), across four pairings and three unrestricted tutors, so the tutored kill is usually one turn away once either half sticks. Deflecting Swat (free post-Edgar) and the white removal protect that turn; against a known combo seat there is a real argument for an earlier, unprotected Edgar purely to switch the free interaction on. You are the beatdown in this matchup and must present the kill first — and prefer presenting the stack-005 all-enchantment pairing, the one their creature interaction cannot break mid-loop.
